GIT BUS FACTOR CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

If one person left tomorrow, which folders would nobody understand?

Paid tools such as CodeScene and Hercules answer this from your repository history. This page does the core of it for free: paste a git log and get a recency-weighted bus factor for every folder, with orphaned folders (the main contributor has gone quiet) and single-owner folders (one active person, no backup) listed first, and who to pair with.

Nothing is uploaded. The log you paste is read in this browser and never leaves your device, and this tool makes no network calls of its own. It is a heuristic from commit history, not a measure of who understands the code.

1. Export your history

Run this inside your own repository and paste everything it prints:

git log --no-merges --since=2.years --format='@@|%an|%ae|%at' --numstat

It lists author names, emails, commit times and changed file paths, so scan it before sharing it with anyone. Here it stays on your device.

2. Paste it

Paste a git log above and click Analyse.

Findings

FolderStatusBus factorMain ownerPair with

Prefer a CLI, or want this in your own CI?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file. It runs git log on your machine and nothing else:

python3 busfactor.py                        # analyse the repo in the current directory
python3 busfactor.py path/to/repo --depth 3  # folders three levels deep
python3 busfactor.py --format json           # machine-readable
python3 busfactor.py --fail-on-orphaned      # exit 2 if a folder lost its owner

Get busfactor.py from the repo — stdlib only, nothing to install, no network calls. Options: --since, --half-life, --inactive-days, --min-commits.

Common questions

What is a bus factor?

The bus factor, or truck factor, is the smallest number of people who would have to leave a project before it stalls because nobody left knows the code. A bus factor of 1 means a single departure is enough. This tool computes it per folder as the fewest contributors whose recency-weighted changes add up to half of the folder's total.

How is ownership calculated here?

Each commit adds the lines it added and deleted in a folder, capped at 500 per file so one giant change cannot own a folder, and halves in weight every 180 days so recent work counts for more. Bots, lock files and vendored or minified files are ignored. The folder's bus factor is how many top contributors it takes to reach half the total.

What do orphaned and single-owner mean?

Orphaned means the person with the largest share of a folder has made no commit anywhere in the last 90 days, so the folder's main knowledge holder may be gone. Single-owner means one still-active person holds at least 80 percent of a folder, so it has no real backup yet. The report names the most active other contributor to pair with.

Does this tool send my git history anywhere?

No. It makes no network calls at all. The log you paste is analysed in this page and never leaves your device; the CLI only runs git log on your own machine.

Does a high bus factor mean my team understands the code?

No. This is a heuristic from commit history, not a measure of who understands the code. Reviewers, pair programmers, documentation, squashed commits, shared accounts and people who left the company under another email all change the real answer. Treat it as a prompt for a conversation, not a verdict about any person.

More: what is a bus factor, and how do you raise it?

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is a heuristic read of commit history, not an assessment of any person's skill or knowledge, and it must not be used on its own to make decisions about hiring, firing, pay or performance. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get busfactor.py from the repo and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. The log you paste is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors, and the tool makes no network calls. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Related checks: Env Example Drift Check finds environment variables your code reads but .env.example does not list, and Required Checks Drift Check finds branch-protection checks that no longer exist.

what-is-bus-factor.html.text:
← Git Bus Factor Check

What is a bus factor (truck factor), and how do you raise it?

The bus factor is the smallest number of people who would have to leave before a project stalls because nobody left understands the code. It is a grim name for a planning question: where is our knowledge held by one head?

How it is measured from git history

Commit history cannot show who understands a file, but it shows who changed it. This tool adds up, per folder, the lines each person added and deleted. A single commit is capped at 500 lines per file so a generated or vendored dump cannot own a folder, and each change loses half its weight every 180 days so recent work counts for more. Bots, lock files, node_modules, vendor, dist and minified files are ignored. The folder's bus factor is the fewest people whose weighted changes reach half of its total. This is a heuristic line scan of history, not a measure of understanding.

The three statuses

  • orphaned — the largest contributor to a folder (at least half of it) has made no commit anywhere in the last 90 days. They may have left, moved teams or be on long leave. Find out, and assign an owner.
  • single-owner — one still-active person holds at least 80 percent of a folder. Nothing is wrong today; one absence away from a problem.
  • shared — more than one person carries the folder, or no one dominates it.

Five ways to raise it

  1. Make the second person the reviewer on the next change in every single-owner folder.
  2. Pair on one real change there instead of scheduling a handover meeting.
  3. Write down what history cannot show: why it was built this way, how it is deployed, where the credentials live.
  4. Hand the next bug or on-call rotation for that area to someone new.
  5. Re-run the check monthly and watch the flagged list shrink; python3 busfactor.py --fail-on-orphaned works as a CI gate.

What this number does not tell you

Squashed commits credit one author for a team's work, pair programming credits one of two people, a contributor who commits under two emails counts as two, and an expert who reviews but rarely commits is invisible. Use the output to start a conversation about a folder, never to judge a person.

No warranty. Provided free and as-is. It is a heuristic and must not be used on its own to make decisions about hiring, firing, pay or performance. Best-effort hosting, no SLA. The page makes no network calls and uploads nothing. Run the check.
